transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Um… yeah. I guess what finally made me come in is my eating has started feeling really out of hand, especially after work or after class. Like I’ll get home and sit down with my laptop, thinking I’m just going to have dinner or maybe watch something while I eat, and then somehow it turns into… a lot more than I meant.

It’s not just a normal meal. I’ll have, like, a whole takeout meal, and then I’ll keep going—chips, something sweet, random snacks I keep in my desk drawer, whatever is nearby. And it feels embarrassing to say, but it’s way more than I’d eat if someone else were there watching me. I don’t usually plan for it to happen like that, but once I’m alone and settled in, it just kind of becomes this whole thing, and afterward I’m like, “Why did I eat all of that?” That’s basically why I’m here.
After these episodes of overeating, do you ever try to compensate for it by making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or exercising excessively?

I’m… not totally sure how to answer that cleanly. I don’t, like, have a routine where I do something afterward to “undo” it, if that’s what you mean. I’ve definitely had the thought after, like, “I shouldn’t eat tomorrow,” or “I need to be better,” but in terms of the specific things you said—making myself throw up or taking laxatives or doing some intense workout right after—I don’t really have something like that to tell you.

I mostly just feel awful and sort of sit with it, honestly. Like I’ll be uncomfortable and embarrassed and tell myself I’m going to fix it somehow, but it doesn’t really turn into one of those behaviors you listed.
During these episodes when you eat more than you plan to, would you say you feel like you can’t stop eating or control what you’re eating once you start?

Yeah… yes, that’s probably the biggest part of why it scares me. It’s not just that I eat a lot, it’s that once it starts, it feels like I can’t really interrupt it.

Like I’ll be sitting there, and part of my brain is very clearly saying, Jaime, stop. You have that budget report to finish, you’re not even hungry anymore, and honestly you’re not even enjoying this now. But then I’m still reaching for the next thing anyway. It’s almost like I’m watching myself do it from a little distance, if that makes sense. I know I’ve already had enough, I know I’m going to feel bad about it, and I still keep going.

And it’s not even always because the food tastes amazing or anything. Sometimes by that point I’m just sort of… continuing. Like I’ll think, okay, after this handful I’m done, and then I’ll open something else, or I’ll go back to the kitchen again. It feels really hard to stop once I’m in that mode.
Do you usually eat these larger amounts of food alone, and if so, is it because you feel embarrassed about how much you’re eating?

Yeah… I do. I mean, not every single bite of food I eat is alone, obviously, but the times where it turns into those really big, out-of-control amounts, I pretty much make sure I’m by myself.

I’ve noticed I kind of wait for the right window, like when my roommate is out or busy, or if I’m at home, when my family has gone to bed. And I hate saying that because it sounds so sneaky, but it really is like I don’t want anyone to see it happening. During the day I’m usually trying to seem like I have everything together, and I’ll talk about being healthy or organized or responsible, and then at night it’s like this totally different thing.

I think I’m embarrassed because if someone saw the actual amount, like the containers or wrappers or how fast it happens, they’d look at me differently. So yes, I eat those larger amounts alone on purpose, because I’m ashamed of how much it is.
Has this pattern of eating affected your daily life in any way—like making you avoid social situations, feel depressed or anxious, or interfere with your work or relationships?

Yeah… it has. I think that’s actually one of the parts that makes me feel most embarrassed, because it’s not just happening and then disappearing, you know? It sort of changes how I act around people.

I’ve been avoiding plans more, especially anything with food involved. Like my friends sometimes do these cooking nights, or my family will want to have dinner together or make something at home, and I’ll come up with some excuse not to go or I’ll say I’m busy with school or work. And part of me really does want to go, but then I get anxious that if I’m around food with other people, they’ll somehow notice something is off. Not even necessarily in the moment, but like they’ll be able to tell I’ve been eating a lot privately, or they’ll watch how much I take, or they’ll make some comment and I’ll just feel exposed.

So I’ve been more isolated outside of work and school. I still show up for the things I have to do, mostly, but socially I’ve pulled back. It’s like I’m trying to keep this whole part of my life hidden, and that takes up more energy than I expected.

latest_inference.note: The patient's description of recurrent episodes of binge eating, feeling a lack of control during eating, eating until uncomfortably full, eating alone due to embarrassment, and significant distress about the behavior meets the diagnostic criteria for Binge Eating Disorder (F50.01). There is no evidence of compensatory behaviors such as purging, misuse of laxatives, or excessive exercise, which rules out Bulimia Nervosa (F50.90).
